articles.title: Trump administration proposes major 2030 census changes: What to know
articles.summary: The Trump administration proposed to change the national census to only count U.S. citizens and permanent residents and exclude immigrants living in the country illegally ahead of the 2030 census. The Census Bureau released the proposal online Wednesday, more than a year after President Trump directed the Commerce Department, which oversees the bureau, to develop…
articles.body:
The Trump administration proposed to change the national census to only count U.S. citizens and permanent residents and exclude immigrants living in the country illegally ahead of the 2030 census.

The Census Bureau released the proposal online Wednesday, more than a year after President Trump directed the Commerce Department , which oversees the bureau, to develop a new census that did not count those who entered the country illegally in the total.

The proposal is seeking to change its definition of a person’s “usual residence” to exclude some immigrants who are legally in the U.S. on a temporary basis, or individuals whose lawful status to be in the country is “less durable and indefinite” than a green card.

Under the 14th Amendment, seats in the House of Representatives must be apportioned by “counting the whole number of persons in each State.” The census has generally counted a person’s residence to determine its count instead of citizenship or immigration status.

The administration argued that in its best interpretation of the Constitution, the term “persons” did not include people living in the U.S. unlawfully, and it argued that immigrants living in the country unlawfully should not count because of “their lack of a sufficient tie and allegiance” to the U.S.

In a separate change, the bureau proposed to eliminate questions about race and ethnicity from the census — information that has been collected since the first census in 1790.

Race and ethnicity data are used by states during redistricting and by the federal government to help enforce measures such as the Voting Rights Act and other civil rights laws.

In the Federal Register notice , the administration defended the change, citing what it described as the potentially “sensitive nature” of the topic and its questions, and a “reduced need for or usefulness of this information” in census data.

The census, conducted every 10 years, is used to determine how the 435 seats in the House are divided among the states. The figures are also used to draw congressional and state legislative districts, and they help determine how federal funding is distributed.

Trump, who will not be president during the 2030 census, previously sought to change the 2020 census and pushed to include a citizenship status question.

The Supreme Court ruled against Trump , finding that the administration did not adequately justify adding the citizenship question to the 2020 census.

articles.title: Trump pledges $500 Obamacare refund checks to 1 million Americans
articles.summary: Eligible Americans in 30 states would begin receiving payments in October, funded by a surplus of fees, the White House said.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has promised to send $500 (£370) to nearly one million Americans, as refunds for what he described as "Obamacare overcharges" collected during the Biden administration.

The refunds, to be sent out starting in October, will go to people in 30 states who buy health insurance through the federal marketplace and do not receive financial help, according to the White House.

Officials said the payments were meant to refund Americans who faced higher premiums and who paid the full cost of their plans.

The promised refunds are on top of the $5,000 payments Trump recently pledged to send Americans if Republicans win control of Congress in November's elections.

Obamacare, formally known as the Affordable Care Act, is the health law passed in 2010 that expanded access to insurance and set national rules for coverage.

It created online marketplaces where people can buy private health plans, often with government assistance that reduces monthly costs.

The marketplaces are operated either by individual states or by the federal government, and people who buy plans through the federal exchange pay monthly premiums. Those who do not qualify for income-based subsidies pay the full cost themselves, which can run to hundreds of dollars a month.

In a fact sheet released on Thursday, the White House said that these consumers were "most exposed" to marketplace "user fees" that it said were added to premiums.

It went on to say that fees collected under President Joe Biden were "far in excess of what was needed to run the exchange", and had created a surplus.

The fact sheet did not say how large the surplus was, or if there were plans to lower fees and premiums in the near future.

While most Democratic lawmakers have not yet responded to the announcement, they have previously defended the law as a key source of affordable health coverage.

Trump attempted to repeal Obamacare in his first term, and in his second has sought to change it. He has repeatedly called for it to be replaced, although he has not outlined a detailed alternative. The rebate plan marks one of his most direct actions involving the law since returning to office.

Medicaid, public health insurance for lower-income people, and Affordable Care Act marketplace enrolment has fallen by about 8 million people since Trump returned to office.

However, the law's largest coverage-related changes under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBA) are not yet in effect and are expected to take several years to be fully implemented.

Payments would cover people in states including Florida, Texas, North Carolina, Ohio, Michigan, and Wisconsin. Cheques will be mailed directly to eligible households, the administration said.

DHS acknowledges that some of these petitioners may incur a temporary loss of productivity due to labor turnover," the rule proposal reads. articles.title: Appeals court denies Trump administration’s mail ballot restrictions
articles.summary: A federal appeals court on Thursday upheld a block on the Trump administration’s restrictions on mail-in voting, as the Supreme Court considers the case. Three judges on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 1st Circuit concurred with U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani, who last week blocked the U.S. Postal Service from implementing President Trump’s…
articles.body:
A federal appeals court on Thursday upheld a block on the Trump administration’s restrictions on mail-in voting, as the Supreme Court considers the case.

Three judges on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 1st Circuit concurred with U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani, who last week blocked the U.S. Postal Service from implementing President Trump’s executive order on mail-in ballots ahead of the November midterms.

That executive order , which Trump signed in the spring, instructed the service to send mail-in ballots only to residents of states that have submitted a list of eligible voters to the administration.

Despite having voted by mail himself, the president has long claimed the practice is rife with fraud, without providing substantive evidence. In blocking Trump’s order last Friday, Talwani wrote there was “no evidence relating to fraudulent mail voting” to support the implementation of the Postal Service’s directive.

Judges Seth Aframe, Gustavo Gelpí Jr. and Julie Rikelman of the 1st Circuit Court agreed with that assessment, writing, “There is no record evidence of past fraud or a likelihood of impending fraud related to” the upcoming midterms.

“Thus, we see no obvious error in the district court’s conclusion that allowing this Final Rule to be effective for the soon-arriving November 3 election will likely result in the disenfranchisement of millions of voters across the country while providing minimal — if any — gains in combating voter fraud,” the judges, all appointees of former President Biden, wrote in a nine-page order .

Talwani, an appointee of former President Obama, has blocked Trump’s order three times during litigation. The Supreme Court overturned her initial block on Aug. 24, ruling Talwani had no authority to rule on a suit Democratic-led states brought against the order before the Postal Service implemented it.

Days later, Talwani barred the administration from going ahead with the mail-in voting restrictions for at least two weeks, ruling the group of blue states and voting rights organizations were likely to succeed in their claims that the policy was unconstitutional.

That was far from the end of the dizzying legal fight over Trump’s executive order. The Department of Justice (DOJ) on Sept. 3 asked the Supreme Court to weigh in on Talwani’s two-week block.

Before the justices could rule on the DOJ’s request, Talwani blocked the Postal Service from implementing the president’s order for a third time on Friday. That led to Solicitor General D. John Sauer sending an updated request to the Supreme Court on Sunday.

In a 40-page emergency application , Sauer argued the administration is likely to succeed on the merits of the cases concerning the policy.

“The Rule ensures that States remain responsible for determining voter eligibility and eligibility to vote by mail, and it does not dictate ballot content, mailing or receipt deadlines, or ballot-counting procedures,” he wrote.

The Supreme Court, which is on recess, will decide the case in an expedited fashion. But complicating matters is the fact that officials in Delaware and North Carolina, two of the states that sued the administration, have already begun mailing ballots to residents.

Seven Republican state election officials have also urged the justices to prevent the administration from implementing the order ahead of Election Day.

In a brief those states and other local election overseers submitted to the court on Wednesday, the officials said the work necessary to implement the Postal Service’s policy “cannot be responsibly accomplished” before the midterms.

articles.title: Jimmy Kimmel moves Senate interview to YouTube in latest collision with FCC
articles.summary: The decision follows a year of surging regulatory hurdles over candidate appearances on the Disney-owned network.
articles.body:
ABC late-night host Jimmy Kimmel has said that an interview with Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico will not air on the network, citing growing intrusion from the Republican-led Federal Communications Commission (FCC) over political candidates’ “equal time” rules.

Talarico is running in Texas against Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton in a race that could decide control of the US Senate in November.

On Wednesday’s broadcast, Kimmel said that he would be interviewing Talarico under “unusual circumstances”, adding that, over the show’s more-than-two-decade run, he had been “interviewing Americans who are running for office with no problem at all”.

But in January, the Republican-led FCC said that daytime and late-night TV talk shows are no longer considered “bona fide” news programmes that are exempt from the equal time rules that require them to give airtime to opposing candidates.

Kimmel noted that for decades talk shows have been free to interview political candidates without being subject to those rules, including interviewing United States President Donald Trump during his 2016 presidential campaign.

“Now that he is president, [Trump’s] FCC threatened me, threatened our show, threatened our network ⁠ABC, our affiliates, our local stations, based on simple traditional editorial decisions — guest bookings it would ⁠seem they don’t like,” Kimmel said.

The interview with Talarico is instead set to be released on YouTube on Thursday.

The Cook Political Report and University of Virginia’s Center for Politics rate the Texas Senate race as a toss-up. An August poll by the Barbara Jordan Public Policy Research and Survey Center at Texas Southern University showed Talarico nosing narrowly ahead of Paxton, 47 percent to 45 percent, among likely voters.

Republicans have stepped up efforts to shore up the seat. Earlier this week, MAGA Inc, the political group aligned with Trump, committed $10m to advertising against Talarico, in what has been described as the first advertisement buy that Trump’s well-heeled political machine has made for a general election.

The move underscores just how much the party’s usually safest bastion, Texas, has emerged as an Achilles’ heel in Republicans’ effort to retain the Senate.

Talarico, 37, is a former public-school teacher who has built his political identity around a progressive interpretation of Christianity.

Democrats see the eighth-generation Texan as a promising vehicle for breaking their decades-long Senate drought in the state. Texas has not elected a Democrat to the chamber since 1988.

The ABC episode unfolds just as Republicans gather in Dallas for the closing ceremony of a highly unorthodox midterm convention — unprecedented in its timing — in what many observers have called a “Trump-a-palooza” parade, with the president commandeering the spotlight as the party seeks to galvanise its base.

Over the past year, The View, Saturday Night Live, Jimmy Kimmel Live! and other programmes have been subjected to heightened FCC supervision over whether their political coverage and candidate appearances comply with federal equal-time rules.

Critics say the agency’s expanding reach into programming decisions risks chilling broadcasters’ editorial independence.

That precarity is compounded by the consolidation of US media ownership. In August, the FCC voted to scrap its 39 percent cap on local television ownership, a move critics warned could concentrate still more control over the country’s broadcast news in fewer corporate hands. That was followed in January by changes to the equal time rules.

The shift has already ensnared Talarico.

The FCC opened an inquiry into his appearance on ABC’s The View in February, while CBS declined to broadcast an interview he had recorded for The Late Show with Stephen Colbert. Colbert subsequently released the interview online.

In April, FCC Chairman Brendan Carr ordered early licence reviews for eight ABC-owned stations — an extraordinary step given that their licences were not due for renewal until 2028.

Network parent company Disney and ABC assailed the probe, arguing it threatened protected speech and upended longstanding constitutional precedents, separately accusing the FCC of using its regulatory authority to intimidate media organisations critical of Trump.

The intimidation tactics had already made the leap from regulatory threats to targeted reprisal in September of last year for Kimmel, as ABC shelved his show indefinitely, before resuming it six days later.

It came as Kimmel’s remarks about the killing of conservative activist Charlie Kirk drew criticism from FCC’s Carr, who urged local broadcasters not to air the programme.

articles.title: Pentagon witness blasts Virginia school district's 'vanilla' 9/11 teacher guide
articles.summary: Fairfax County, Va., schools face criticism over its new 9/11 guide, which identifies al Qaeda but emphasizes Muslim sensitivities and warns teachers not to “center the extremists."
articles.body: A wealthy Washington, D.C., suburb's public school district is advising teachers not to link 9/11 with radical Islam and to be sure to create "safe spaces" for Muslim students as the nation somberly marks the 25th anniversary of the terror attacks that killed nearly 3,000 Americans. The guardrails in a six-page instructional guide, "25th Anniversary and Commemoration of 9/11" and distributed to teachers, has prompted critics to accuse Fairfax County (Virginia) Public School's liberal leaders of coddling post-9/11 sensitivities rather than teaching history. s"It's sort of a vanilla way to do things," retired Navy Vice Admiral Lou Crenshaw, who was stationed inside the Pentagon when al Qaeda terrorists crashed a hijacked passenger jet into the building. "Everybody can go through the deal and feel good about it. And at the end of the day, nobody complains. CBC TELLS JOURNALISTS NOT TO CALL 9/11 ‘TERRORIST ATTACKS’ IN INTERNAL GUIDANCE "To me, that's not exactly what we need to do. We need to make sure that the kids have learned a lesson here. And that's not going to happen if we try to shave the facts to the point where it's hard to figure out what we're talking about." A digital content analysis reveals that about half of the 1,740-word document is devoted to tips for creating "safe spaces for Muslim and Middle Eastern students," about 15% spells out specific 9/11 instruction and the rest of the document tip-toes around managing "emotional responses" to the lesson. The guide by the school district, which sits only a few miles from the Pentagon and several military bases, mentions military families only three times and first responders only once, saying at one point, "Many families of military personnel and first responders experienced loss and hardship." Meanwhile, it has 30 references to Islam, "Muslim families," "Muslim students," "anti-Muslim racism," "anti-Middle Eastern" rhetoric, "Islamophobic rhetoric" and "Middle Eastern students" and families. It includes a bulleted list of "critical considerations" to challenge anti-Muslim bias. The curriculum guidance speaks to a wider tension about how the 9/11 attacks are described by influential figures from teachers, journalists and politicians to social media influencers as a network of powerful Muslim organizations have built educational programs over the past 25 years downplaying discussions about the extremist interpretations of Islam that motivated al Qaeda and the 19 hijackers involved in the 9/11 attacks. On Thursday, New York Police Department Commissioner Jessica Tisch called for "moral clarity" about what happened on 9/11, saying in a speech, "The men who attacked this city were terrorists. The men and women who ran into the towers to save innocent lives were heroes. "Twenty-five years cannot be allowed to blur that distinction, and shame on those who do." Last month, after a major public backlash, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation reversed earlier guidance that instructed journalists to avoid calling 9/11 a "terrorist attack." In a statement provided to Fox News Digital, Fairfax County Public Schools said the school community has a "deeply personal connection to September 11 because of our proximity to the Pentagon and the many military-connected families we serve. "On the 25th anniversary of the terrorist attacks, we remember the nearly 3,000 people who were killed, including 184 at the Pentagon. We remember the victims, their families, the survivors, and everyone whose lives were forever changed. We honor the first responders whose courage and sacrifice continue to inspire us," the school district said. "FCPS remains committed to creating an inclusive environment in our schools where all students feel welcome and respected as we strive to provide a world-class education and workplace." articles.title: Trump gifts 4 aides $45K each as Americans struggle
articles.summary: $45,000 is not pocket change. For many Americans, that could erase high-interest debt, cover months of housing, fund child care, build an emergency savings cushion or become a down payment.
articles.body:
President Trump gave four White House aides a total of $155,000 in cash holiday gifts last year, according to new financial disclosures.

Who got the money? Well, Natalie Harp, Margo Martin and Chamberlain Harris received $45,000 a piece. Walt Nauta received $20,000.

Harp, Martin and Harris each make $150,000 a year. So that $45,000 “gift” equals 30 percent of their annual government salary — roughly three-and-a-half months of pay — handed over in cash directly from the president.

The White House says Trump has a longstanding practice of giving Christmas gifts to people in his orbit, and insists these payments had nothing to do with their official duties and were therefore permissible.

But federal law tells a different story.

Government employees generally can’t get extra compensation from a private person for doing their government job. The idea is to make sure their paycheck and their loyalty comes from the government and not from someone who has power over them.

The law exists in part to prevent outside money, like in this case, from influencing a public employee’s loyalty.

Former White House ethics lawyer Richard Painter told The New York Times these payments appear to raise exactly that problem.

Let’s go back to who got these big holiday bonuses. Natalie Harp is Trump’s executive assistant, famously dubbed the “human printer” because she carries a portable printer to give him favorable media coverage and social-media posts. She was also among the aides involved when Trump secretly left Air Force One during a security threat in Turkey.

Margo Martin has worked with Trump since his first presidency, followed him to Palm Beach after the 2020 election and returned to the White House after his 2024 victory.

Chamberlain Harris is deputy director of Oval Office operations and serves on the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts, which has been heavily involved in the White House ballroom project.

And Walt Nauta is the current director of Oval Office operations. He was also the guy who was charged alongside Trump in the classified-documents case — charges that were dismissed in 2024. So you could say he’s Trump’s “ride or die.”

Now let’s talk about the amount of money these folks were given. $45,000 is not pocket change. For many Americans, that could erase high-interest debt, cover months of housing, fund child care, build an emergency savings cushion or become a down payment.

Imagine being another federal employee who got no bonus because you weren’t blindly allegiant to the president. Better yet, imagine all of the teachers, nurses, warehouse workers, farmers, military families or parents who are working just as hard and watching the cost of housing, food and insurance eat up more of their paycheck with each decision the administration makes.

We are watching a president whose personal wealth and business interests remain intertwined with the presidency. A president who is personally handing tens of thousands of dollars to the government employees closest to him. Even if you set aside the ethics questions and the legal implications involved, it’s clear that everyone who is not in Trump’s inner circle, every average American, will be paying the bills he’s left the country with as he and his closest allies continue to profit.

Lindsey Granger is a NewsNation contributor and co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising.” This column is an edited transcription of her on-air commentary.

articles.title: Brazil's Supreme Court cancels session as political crisis deepens
articles.summary: Brazil's Supreme Court canceled a second consecutive session of deliberations on Thursday, a rare step that highlights its deep institutional and political c...
articles.body:
SAO PAULO (AP) — Brazil's Supreme Court canceled a second consecutive session of deliberations on Thursday, a rare step that highlights its deep institutional and political crisis .

Suspicions of graft, political bias and police interference loom over several of its members, and the turmoil is already spilling into October's national elections.

Chief-Justice Luiz Edson Fachin ordered the cancellation Thursday, reconvening for Tuesday, when the court is not usually in session. The full court of 10 justices will analyze whether one of them, Alexandre de Moraes, should be investigated for alleged links to the owner of failed Banco Master, which was shuttered after allegations of fraud.

The turmoil at the court erupted on Sept. 1 with Justice André Mendonca, a Bolsonaro appointee, unsealing federal police documents that showed banker Daniel Vorcaro repeatedly sought legal advice from de Moraes . The animosity between de Moraes and Mendonca has only grown since.

De Moraes, a conservative, was hailed as a hero by Lula supporters after he sentenced former President Jair Bolsonaro to 27 years in prison last year for an attempted coup. Mendonca was Bolsonaro's solicitor-general before reaching Brazil's top court.

Earlier this week, de Moraes shot back and requested an inquiry into an alleged abuse of power by Mendonca for interviewing the banker without the presence of policemen or prosecutors.

Both President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and his rival in the upcoming elections — the former president's son, Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro — are now demanding investigations into the Supreme Court justices, along party lines.

Brazil's federal police leadership is also at stake, as competing Supreme Court decisions this week removed and then reinstated its director-general, also as part of the cross fire between justices.

Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) on Thursday circulated a fundraising text springboarding off his surprise video appearance at the GOP midterm convention in Dallas, a cameo that has triggered the fury of some of Fetterman’s Democratic critics.

The fundraising text highlights his bipartisan work with Republican Sen. Dave McCormick (R-Pa.) and links to an ActBlue fundraising webpage with the video of Fetterman that Republicans played in Dallas embedded in it.

In the video, a C-SPAN clip of Fetterman’s speech introducing McCormick at the convention, he tells the audience that he’s a “commonsense Democrat” who “is always going to stand with America” and “always going to reject the extremes in socialism and that anti-American way of life.”

The ActBlue fundraising blurb below the video says Fetterman “came to Washington to fight for Pennsylvania’s working people, forgotten communities and families to get ahead.”

“He’ll keep standing his ground, speaking his mind and putting Pennsylvania first,” it says.

The webpage gives potential donors the option to give $5 to $250 or to write in a custom amount to support Fetterman.

The convention appearance has drawn pushback from some Democrats, such as Pennsylvania Rep. Madeleine Dean (D), who called it a “stunt” and “gravely disappointing.”

articles.body:
( The Hill ) — Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is trolling his Republican opponent, former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.), over his appearance at the GOP midterm convention in Dallas via a video game.

The retro-style game’s start screen features the game’s title, “COME HOME, MIKE,” and Rogers’ face superimposed on a cartoon body standing on a boat in water.

“Help Mike Rogers find his way from Florida back to Michigan,” text on the start screen reads. “(He hasn’t managed it yet).”

Below the start button, instructions tell the player to “drag Mike’s yacht” and “answer three questions to unlock the doors home.”

Once the game begins, the player starts in Cape Coral, Florida, shown as a pixelated sandy beach with a palm tree. Those playing the game have to direct Rogers, on his boat, through a maze on water to get to a football field in Michigan.

Football has become a contentious issue in the race , with Rogers accusing El-Sayed of being against the sport and El-Sayed challenging Rogers to a tackle football game in lieu of a debate, which he claims Rogers is ducking.

El-Sayed has slammed Rogers before for moving to Florida after leaving the House, telling the former representative “if you want to be a Florida man, go be a Florida man” last month.

In the video game, Rogers and his occasional boat hit a roadblock where the player is forced to make a choice between a “yes” and “no” option. However, the “yes” option is never actually available.

“Mike, Michiganders are really struggling with the cost of prescription drugs,” one of the roadblock prompts reads. “Will you agree to vote to lower prescription drug prices when you get to the Senate?”

After the last roadblock, access to the “Michigan” endpoint is restricted, and the player is directed to the midterm convention in Dallas.

Rogers is speaking at the GOP midterm convention in Dallas on Thursday evening, while other Republicans in contentious Senate races are skipping the event amid Trump’s slumping approval ratings, the ongoing Iran War and Democrats’ recent surge in the generic congressional ballot.

Rogers responded to the Michigan Democrat’s jab in a statement shared with The Hill Thursday, saying, “while [El-Sayed] plays games, we’ll keep talking to Michiganders.”

“We’ve got a state to save,” the Rogers campaign added.

In his statement, the Michigan Republican also noted a rental property El-Sayed’s wife reportedly owns in Dubai, according to The Detroit News.

articles.title: US appeals court rejects Trump bid to implement new vote-by-mail rules
articles.summary: The ruling is a blow to Trump administration’s efforts to change how mail-in voting works ahead of November elections.
articles.body:
A United States appeals court has declined to allow the administration of President Donald Trump to implement controversial new rules about how mail-in voting is conducted, with less than eight weeks left before the November 3 midterm elections.

On Thursday, the First Circuit Court of Appeals in Boston, Massachusetts, decided against lifting an injunction against the rules, issued by a lower court last week.

The US Supreme Court is currently weighing a similar request.

At issue are a set of finalised rules released by the US Postal Service (USPS) in late August that would place new requirements on mail-in balloting.

The rules direct states to redesign mail-in ballots to include unique barcodes that can be scanned, so that the federal government may track them.

States would also be required to submit a list of voters slated to receive ballots by mail. The Postal Service would retain the right to “not transmit mail-in or absentee ballots” if the mail-outs do not comply with the new standards or if the voters in question do not appear on the submitted lists.

The case heard on Thursday involved a coalition of voting rights advocacy groups, including the League of Women Voters.

They argued that the new rules, championed by Trump, a Republican, would effectively disenfranchise certain voters who rely on mail-in ballots.

But the Trump administration has argued that the rules are necessary to ensure election security.

In asking the appeals court to lift the injunction, the ‌US Department of Justice argued that the plaintiffs’ case appeared to be based on an unfounded premise that Postal Service intends to seize control of election administration.

It emphasised that state election officials ‌would ‌retain full control over who is permitted to vote by mail and that the Postal Service’s role would be limited to ensuring that envelopes for the mail-in ballots comply with the “modest” new design requirements.

The appeals court, however, denied the Trump administration’s motion to dismiss the injunction, citing the potential for confusion ahead of the midterm vote.

It also affirmed parts of the lower-court ruling, issued by US District Judge Indira Talwani, an appointee of Democratic President Barack ⁠Obama.

“The district court made detailed findings about the chaos and widespread disenfranchisement that would occur between now and November 3 should the Final Rule take immediate effect,” the appeals court said in Thursday’s decision.

It cited issues including that “it would be impossible for some States to reprint compliant envelopes” and that the Postal Service would face the “herculean task” of scanning “tens of millions of ballot envelopes” using a digital portal that is not yet functional.

“There is no countervailing record evidence disputing the district court’s findings on these points,” the appeals court added.

Under the US Constitution, election administration falls to the states. But Trump has pushed for greater voting restrictions ahead of the pivotal midterms, in an effort to combat alleged election fraud.

Critics, however, have framed his actions as an effort to sway the outcome. Currently, Trump’s Republican Party holds majorities in both chambers of Congress. But with Trump facing drooping poll numbers, Democrats are seeking to flip Congress to their control.

All 50 US states allow ⁠for some form of mail-in voting. Twenty-nine states allow voters to ask to cast ballots by mail without providing a reason, and eight conduct their elections entirely ⁠by mail.

The legal battle over the mail-in ballots has stretched on for weeks, creating uncertainty ahead of the vote.

In addition to the voting advocacy groups challenging the new rules, a group of 24 states, plus the District of Columbia, have also filed a lawsuit.

Last month, the US Supreme Court lifted an earlier injunction issued by Judge Talwani blocking the rules from taking effect.

The Trump administration last week once again made an emergency petition to the high court to intervene and pause Talwani’s ruling.

The new rules came after Trump issued an executive order in March calling for tighter rules to govern voting by mail.

Trump has also repeatedly pushed the false claim that his defeat in the 2020 presidential election was the result of widespread voter fraud.

An anonymous whistleblower statement released ⁠on September 1 by Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal alleged that the Postal Service had rushed to implement the new rules, but that the result was a faulty system that risks disrupting the delivery of mail-in ballots.

Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, plans to introduce legislation that would codify the dividend checks and wants it done as soon as the upcoming midterm elections are over, when the balance of power could tilt in favor of Democrats. But the money, Moreno told Fox News Digital, wouldn’t come from taxpayers’ coffers. Instead, he wants to approve certain structural tariffs to act as a "market access fee" that would find its way back into the pockets of Americans. TRUMP DEFENDS $5,000 DIVIDEND PROPOSAL, PRAISES 'BEAUTIFUL' TARIFFS ON 'INGRAHAM ANGLE' And it can only be spent in the U.S. "This dividend would be something that is allowing working Americans to share in the prosperity of this country," Moreno said. "The money would be used only here in the United States, so it's not to be used outside the United States. I think it would provide a big economic boost to our economy." "So, if you're a company out there, anywhere in the world, you want to sell your products in America, you either make it here in the United States, or you pay a fee to enter our market," he continued. "That money goes to funding this one-time dividend." Trump floated the plan Wednesday night during the Republicans’ midterm convention in Dallas, where the GOP and several — but not all — vulnerable incumbents and candidates flocked to energize their base and pitch why they should maintain control of Congress. TRUMP JUST EXPANDED HIS TARIFF PLAYBOOK WITH A POWERFUL TRADE WEAPON NO PRESIDENT HAS EVER USED The cost, however, could be an eye-popping $1.2 trillion. Moreno argued that the cost was worth it and noted that despite the steps Republicans have taken to lower costs, Americans are still feeling the crunch. "It's about providing relief," Moreno said. "It's acknowledgment that during the Biden years, it was so bad for working families, that, despite what we've already done in 18 months, it just isn't enough to get working families to basically so that they're level, right?" "Because they're underwater right now," he continued. "I think it's extremely important for us to understand in elected office that working families are struggling." For the plan to work, Republicans would need to maintain their control of both chambers of Congress, and it comes as the nation’s federal deficit skyrocketed to $40 trillion last month and as the GOP has consistently pitched itself as the party of fiscal responsibility against Democrats’ wanton federal spending. Trump's plan scored one unlikely ally in House Freedom Caucus Chairman Andy Harris, R-Md., leader of a pack of fiscal hawks who routinely scoff at Congress’ inability to tackle the nation’s debt. "Hardworking American taxpayers probably deserve a tax rebate. We're gonna have to discuss, you know, how large a rebate that would be. But I think, again, American taxpayers deserve relief from taxation. I think that's a good idea," Harris told Fox News Digital in an interview during the GOP midterm convention. REPUBLICAN SOUNDS ALARM ON RISING DEM STAR: 'THIS GUY’S GOING TO BE A PROBLEM' Harris said such a plan "would have to go through Congress," and he suggested that the party-line budget reconciliation process would be needed to skirt Democratic opposition. The Senate’s top Republican agreed with Harris. "It smells very much like a reconciliation issue," Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told Fox News Digital. Thune said Senate Republicans would be willing to work with Trump and his team to get the dividends done, but noted that until Wednesday night it was a proposal that "we hadn’t heard before." He argued that the idea showed the difference between the GOP and Democrats seeking power. "I think it illustrates the clear contrast between us and the Democrats about how you want to, how you see government functioning," Thune said. "And one is in giving more power, control, money in the pockets of the American people, and the other, giving more power to, you know, for people in Washington to tell you how to run your life." And Republicans will likely have to rely on reconciliation to do it, given that Democrats are already slamming the idea. "Donald Trump is a known liar. This is the biggest liar to ever serve in government, period. And look, the dividend is not happening," Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., told Fox News Digital. "He promised a dividend on tariffs, that didn't happen. He promised a dividend on Doge, that didn't happen. He promised some strange new dividend from Air Force One, what, six months ago. That never happened." Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., recoiled and slammed the move as emblematic of Trump’s presidency being "so failed and broken, he is resorting to trying to bribe the American people for their votes." Moreno countered that when it comes to dumping tens of billions of dollars outside the U.S., Democrats were all on board but didn’t show the same vigor when it came to seeing money flow back into America. "So look, at the end of the day, these politicians are all hypocritical. They love helping anybody on earth except for working Americans," Moreno said. "They love giving money to foreign countries. They love funding endless wars. They love having us solve the entirety of the world's problems. When it comes to helping working Americans, all of a sudden, there's no money. What we're saying is no."

articles.title: Rubio says he has ‘no plans at this time’ to run for president
articles.summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio, whose name has been floated as a possible 2028 Republican contender to succeed President Trump, said he has no plans to launch another bid for the White House. “I don’t know what the future holds, but I have no plans at this time,” Rubio said in an interview with Colombian…
articles.body:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, whose name has been floated as a possible 2028 Republican contender to succeed President Trump, said he has no plans to launch another bid for the White House.

“I don’t know what the future holds, but I have no plans at this time,” Rubio said in an interview with Colombian news station RCN , translated by NBC News. “I’m not a candidate for anything right now. And I’m 100 percent focused on my job, and I have to be because I have two jobs.”

The comments are in line with what one person familiar with the matter told NBC News, telling the outlet that Rubio “loves being secretary of State and is really enjoying the job.” The person said Rubio has no intention of running in 2028.

“If you asked him if he’s interested in 2032 or 2036, he would probably say sure,” the person told the outlet.

Rubio and Vice President Vance, who have talked about their friendship during their time in the Trump administration, have both been suggested as possible torchbearers of Trump’s legacy when his term ends in 2029.

The Hill’s ranking of possible GOP presidential contenders listed Vance as the top candidate to succeed Trump, with Rubio in second place. Neither Republican has said publicly whether they will run for president in 2028 , but they are the consensus top two in recent polls of likely GOP voters .

An Emerson College and The Hill survey released last month showed Rubio outperforming Vance in five match-ups against Democrats, with the exception of former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, who held a 5-point edge against both Republicans.

Rubio first ran for president in the 2016 Republican primaries, launching his campaign the year before.

The former Florida senator pitched himself as a next-generation candidate, heavily emphasizing foreign policy and urging that the U.S. leave its deal with Iran over its nuclear program, which the U.S. would do in 2018 during Trump’s first term.

Rubio later suspended his campaign and backed Trump after losing his home state’s primary to the native New Yorker. He remained in the Senate until Trump, after winning a second term in the 2024 election, tapped Rubio to be his secretary of State.

articles.title: Hillary Clinton warns the U.S. has let its guard down on terrorism 25 years after 9/11
articles.summary: Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton warned Thursday that the Trump administration isn’t doing enough to monitor and thwart terrorists who still pose a threat to the U.S., 25 years after the 9/11 attacks.
articles.body: Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton warned Thursday that the Trump administration isn’t doing enough to monitor and thwart terrorists who still pose a threat to the U.S., 25 years after the 9/11 attacks. “I worry a lot that we’ve let down our guard on counterterrorism, and I don’t say this to scare anybody or to exaggerate, but I think we are not paying enough attention to resurgent terrorist actions,” Clinton said in an interview with NBC News’ Andrea Mitchell at the VOICES 25th Anniversary Symposium, an event reflecting on the attacks. Clinton, who was a U.S. senator from New York on 9/11, said that there have been many “close calls” with terrorist plots in the ensuing quarter century and some that succeeded. “The threat did not go away — it receded — but it is still there, and there are still many thousands of extremists in the world who wish us a great deal of ill,” she said. Clinton argued that the U.S. needs to overcome its internal divisions and confront threats from both nation-state adversaries, like Russia, China and Iran, and nonstate adversaries, like terrorist groups. She lashed out at President Donald Trump for spending so much attention on his planned White House ballroom. “When you’re more interested in building your ballroom than figuring out what the intelligence is coming out of Afghanistan — that is absolutely contrary to any kind of sensible decision-making,” she said. Clinton accused the Trump administration of dismantling parts of the federal government, including within the State Department, that traditionally collected intelligence and evaluated these terrorist threats. As a result, she said, the U.S. doesn’t have “eyes and ears in a lot of these countries,” including in western Africa, where she said extremism is taking hold. The administration cut thousands of jobs across the federal government last year as part of the Elon Musk-led Department of Government Efficiency effort, including at the CIA and the State Department. “I am increasingly concerned because I don’t think we are focused. I know there are very dedicated people still in the government, you know, in the FBI, in the intelligence agencies. I understand that,” she said. “But they don’t have ... the resources, and they’re not given the kind of mission focus that they need right now to adequately do their jobs.” Reached for comment, the White House referred NBC News to the Department of Homeland Security, which didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. During the interview, Clinton also reflected on the revelations about the toxic air quality in Manhattan after 9/11, recalling her experience at ground zero. “It looked like a black curtain,” she said. “There was particulates. ... There was, you know, acrid smells. My throat hurt.” Asked if misleading information about the air from the Bush administration at the time was deliberate, bad science or an effort to reassure the public, Clinton said it was “all three.” “I think that there was a certain element of some leaders being unwilling to face the truth because they wanted to get the economy going,” she said. “They wanted to get Wall Street open. They wanted people to feel like normalcy was possible, and so they either deliberately ignored or they didn’t ask the right questions.” She also responded to Jon Stewart, comedian and 9/11 health advocate, who said that the U.S. has lost nearly 10,000 people to 9/11-related illnesses, which is three times as many people as the nearly 3,000 killed in the twin towers. Addressing the fact that there are people experiencing these health effects that aren’t registered for programs intended to help these victims, Clinton said, “There needs to be a concerted effort to fund this expanded outreach and screening and treatment. And I would hope that the city, the state and the federal government would join together to do that.”

articles.title: Trump faces reckoning as GOP figures label $5K promise a 'socialist vote-buying scheme'
articles.summary: President Donald Trump's $5,000 dividend proposal could cost over $1.2 trillion, sparking a fierce GOP debate over tariff revenue and national debt.
articles.body: President Donald Trump’s proposal to send $5,000 checks to American adults if Republicans win both chambers of Congress is forcing Republicans to debate an idea more commonly associated with the Democratic side of the aisle: sending direct government payments to voters. Called a "socialist vote-buying scheme" by former GOP Rep. Bob Good of Virginia, the so-called Trump Dividend would only be handed down if Republicans keep the House and Senate in November, the president announced at the party's midterm convention in Dallas. Good warned that the checks would add to the national debt, which has topped $40 trillion. The plan could cost more than $1.2 trillion, based on estimates of roughly 240 million eligible adults. The president cannot direct the Treasury to issue the checks without a law providing that authority, so Congress would need to authorize the spending plan. TRUMP MAKES STUNNING FIRST-OF-ITS-KIND CASH PROMISE IN BID TO RALLY GOP VOTERS AT DALLAS MIDTERM CONVENTION "If the Republicans win the House of Representatives and the United States Senate, both of them … I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000," Trump said during his keynote address Wednesday night. He compared the payment to a cash distribution from a successful company to its shareholders and said the money would have to be spent domestically. "The only caveat I have is that the dividend that we're making must be spent in the United States of America," Trump said. "We don't want you going to Canada to spend the money." "If you keep us in power and allow us to continue to do these things, then you’re going to share in some of the benefit of this incredible wealth that we’re creating in the United States of America," Vice President JD Vance said after Trump unveiled his new idea. Conservative commentator Matt Walsh called the plan "flagrant bribery" and said Republicans could help working Americans by allowing them to keep more of their own money through tax cuts. "Holding it as a carrot on the stick for after the election is just shameless," Walsh wrote. Vance and Trump both pointed to tariff revenue as a potential funding source for the payments, and questions emerged over where the money would come from to fund the dividends. "The reason the Democrats can’t do that is because they don’t do tariffs. They don’t take in money. All they know is poverty," Trump said Wednesday night. Treasury data show the federal government collected about $154.4 billion in customs duties from Oct. 1, 2025, through July 31, 2026, which would cover roughly 13% of the estimated $1.2 trillion cost of sending $5,000 checks to about 240 million adults. The administration has not provided an income threshold for the proposed middle-class payments or explained how much tariff revenue would be dedicated to the program. The remaining cost would have to be covered through other federal revenue, spending reductions or additional borrowing. CONGRESS SPENDS $7 TRILLION; HERE’S HOW THAT MATH WORKS OUT IF YOU THINK OF JUST $100 Vance also suggested in an interview after the president's speech Wednesday that the proposal could be limited to middle-class Americans rather than every adult citizen, potentially lowering the cost. The VP defended the idea as "fundamentally a dividend for American workers," arguing that tariffs have generated revenue from foreign companies and countries that have taken advantage of American workers. The proposal’s funding and eligibility questions have fueled criticism from fiscal conservatives, who say the plan would create a new government benefit while adding to the national debt. Rep. Chip Roy, R-Texas, said the estimated $1.2 trillion cost of the dividend proposal could instead be used to eliminate taxes for married parents with dependents earning up to $200,000. "Or maybe some of us think dependency is evil & soul-sucking in all its forms," Roy wrote in a follow-up post. That criticism from Republicans reflects a broader conservative argument that tax cuts are preferable to direct payments because they reduce the government’s role rather than create a new reason for Americans to rely on it. James Fishback, a former Florida gubernatorial candidate who previously proposed a $5,000 DOGE dividend, said his plan would have returned savings generated by spending cuts. Meanwhile, he argued Trump’s proposal would add to the debt without a comparable reduction in government spending. Investor Joe Lonsdale called the idea "bread and circus bribes." Former Arkansas Gov. Asa Hutchinson urged Republican leaders to reject it and focus on reducing the debt. Other Republicans and Trump allies are moving in the opposite direction. Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, said he would prepare legislation to pass the dividend after the election, while Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., asked voters how they would spend their $5,000. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The reactions show a Republican Party split between treating tariff revenue as money to return to Americans and preserving the party’s traditional emphasis on lower taxes, limited spending and less government dependence.

articles.title: DDHQ shifts Senate odds to Democrats, then back to GOP: ‘A coin flip’
articles.summary: The election handicapper Decision Desk HQ on Wednesday briefly shifted its odds of the Democrats winning the Senate to 51 percent, underscoring the party’s growing momentum in the midterm elections. While DDHQ, a partner of The Hill, shifted its odds ever so slightly back in the GOP’s direction on Thursday, giving Republicans a 51 percent…
articles.body:
The election handicapper Decision Desk HQ on Wednesday briefly shifted its odds of the Democrats winning the Senate to 51 percent, underscoring the party’s growing momentum in the midterm elections.

While DDHQ, a partner of The Hill, shifted its odds ever so slightly back in the GOP’s direction on Thursday, giving Republicans a 51 percent chance of winning, it was a notable moment given that Republicans were seen as having a 60 percent chance by DDHQ of retaining the Senate just two months ago.

Since then, President Trump’s approval numbers have hit new lows as oil and gas prices have remained stubbornly high and unhappiness with the economy among voters has become a hallmark of the election season.

“The national environment is more favorable for Democrats, and then on top of that, you have polling data showing that a lot of the sort of must-win or must compete in Senate races for Democrats are pretty 50-50 now,” said Geoffrey Skelley, chief elections analyst at Decision Desk HQ. “When I look at our forecast, we have essentially four states now that are in our sort of toss-up range, but they all have a very very slight Democratic lean.”

All but one state’s primaries are over, meaning all the competitive general election matchups are decided, and polling shows a number of Republican-held seats in serious play for Democrats. Skelley named Maine, Ohio, Texas and Alaska as examples. Iowa is also increasingly thought to be a toss-up, and the Democratic candidate has been leading in the polls to claim the open Senate seat in North Carolina.

Heading into 2026, the Senate was widely seen as likely to remain in GOP hands even if the margins narrowed. Decision Desk HQ had kept an optimistic rating for Republicans throughout much of the summer. As of mid-July, the odds of Republicans keeping the Senate were 60 percent. But that gap has closed significantly, becoming a toss-up around late August and, in recent days, flip-flopping between a slight Republican lean and slight Democrat lean.

Skelley said it’s essentially “a coin flip.”

Other election analysts have similarly determined the Senate majority to be a toss-up: Kyle Kondik at Sabato’s Crystal Ball, an election data tracker out of the University of Virginia, wrote on Sept. 2 that the Senate “is much closer to being a toss-up than the House is” and that while their analysis still favored the GOP’s odds, “that assessment has gotten harder to defend over the course of the summer.”

The nonpartisan Cook Political Report has six Senate seats in its “toss-up” column, five of which are held by Republicans, as well as a GOP-held seat it rates “lean Democratic.”

It’s still early, though. Election analysts at this point in 2024 showed a toss-up or former Vice President Kamala Harris with a slight lead, which did not materialize.

“I do think that, because the Senate map is so favorable for Republicans at sort of baseline, I do think if President Trump were to get his approval rating back up a couple points, that would probably be helpful to the GOP,” said Skelley. “I don’t know if it would change the House dramatically. Democrats are more favored there, but you know, the Senate, because you’re talking about all these red-leaning states where Democrats have to really outperform the 2024 numbers, there is time for some subtle changes that could matter to what’s going on.”

It’s a reality that Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) nodded to last week when he told a local television station that he worried about losing control of the Senate.

“I worry about that, for sure,” he told South Dakota’s KELOLAND News . “I’m a realist, and I just think you, I don’t ever try and sugarcoat things. I think it’s a competitive environment right now. I think we got the highest-quality candidates.”

Republicans and Trump are now pulling out all the messaging stops to rally Republican voters and independents to vote for their local Senate Republican candidate on Nov. 3. At the Republican’s unusual midterm convention in Dallas, Senate leaders lambasted Democrats and described them as “radical” and “dangerous” as much as possible.

Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.), chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee which fundraises for and backs Republican candidates, and Republican Whip John Barrasso (Wyo.) both pitched the battle for the Senate as essential to enacting Trump’s agenda and made the case that the Democratic Senate hopefuls would not support that effort.

Scott ran through a roll call of Democratic candidates in the most competitive Senate races, calling out each over their support of controversial positions like transgender athletes in women’s and girls’ sports.

“The only way to keep dangerous, radical, weird out of the Senate is a united Republican party standing with our President Donald J. Trump,” Scott thundered from the stage.

Trump, in his own speech at the convention, repeated his call for Republicans to “pretend like I’m on the ballot” and promised to give $5,000 to every American adult if Republicans win the House and Senate.

“All they know is poverty and how to ruin our country,” Trump said of Democrats. “But we’re making a fortune. So if the Republicans win, you win with us.”
